title: A Phase Lag Is a Clue

scenes.tts: Rotifers graze on algae in a chemostat. That is a vessel with a steady flow of nutrient medium in, and a matching flow out. Both populations rise and fall in cycles. Watch when the rotifers peak. They peak after the algae do, but how long after? That delay is a clue, and this film asks what it can tell us.
scenes.visual: A chemostat vessel with algae dots and rotifer blobs whose counts rise and fall while two cycle curves trace out beside it; a question bracket marks the delay between the first peaks.
scenes.narration: Rotifers graze on algae in a chemostat. That is a vessel with a steady flow of nutrient medium in, and a matching flow out. Both populations rise and fall in cycles. Watch when the rotifers peak. They peak after the algae do, but how long after? That delay is a clue, and this film asks what it can tell us.

scenes.tts: In classical predator prey models, the predator peak lags the prey peak by about a quarter of a cycle. Prey rise, predators feed and multiply, prey crash, predators starve. The phase lag is the delay between peaks, as a fraction of the cycle's period. Phase lag in cycles equals delay in days over period in days.
scenes.visual: Full-width cycle sketch: a marker steps through the four phases on the two curves, then a delay bracket between the peaks and the formula appear.
scenes.caption: In classical predator-prey models, the predator peak lags the prey peak by about a quarter of a cycle. Prey rise, predators feed and multiply, prey crash, predators starve. The phase lag is the delay between peaks, as a fraction of the cycle's period. Phase lag in cycles equals delay in days over period in days.

scenes.tts: Here is an invented example. Assume the cycles are regular. Prey peak on days ten, forty and seventy, so the period is thirty days. In run A, the rotifers peak on day seventeen and a half. That is seven and a half days after the prey. Seven and a half over thirty is a quarter cycle, the classical lag.
scenes.visual: Invented run A: prey peaks marked on days 10, 40, 70, the period bracket of 30 days, the rotifer peak on day 17.5 and the 7.5 day delay; the arithmetic builds below.

scenes.tts: In run B, the rotifers peak on day twenty five instead. That is fifteen days after the prey. Fifteen over thirty is one half cycle. The predator peaks now sit at the prey troughs. That pattern is called antiphase.
scenes.visual: The rotifer curve slides from run A to run B; delay of 15 days, the sum 15 / 30 = 0.50, and dashed lines show predator peaks sitting at prey troughs.
scenes.caption: In run B, the rotifers peak on day 25 instead. That is 15 days after the prey. 15 over 30 is one half cycle. The predator peaks now sit at the prey troughs. That pattern is called antiphase.

scenes.tts: Yoshida and colleagues grew the rotifer Brachionus on the alga Chlorella. The alga was either one clone or several. One clone cannot evolve by selection among clones. Several can. Single clone prey gave short cycles with the classical quarter lag. Multiclonal prey gave long cycles, with peaks largely out of step. In the real experiment the two treatments did not share a period. In our example, run B resembles the evolving prey runs.
scenes.visual: Two panels side by side: one clone with run A, several clones with run B; notes tie run A to the single clone runs and run B to the evolving prey runs.

scenes.tts: But the lag alone does not prove that the algae evolved. A long lag could have other causes. The causal case came from changing the clonal diversity, and from a measured trade-off. Algae that resisted grazing were poorer competitors for nutrients. The study showed prey evolution. It did not investigate predator evolution. So keep this rule. A phase lag is a pattern. The causal case comes from changing the prey's variation.
scenes.visual: The lag chip points to a prey-evolution box with a red not-proof mark; two experimental findings point to it with solid arrows and turn it green; prey evolution shown, predator evolution not investigated.
